name: Mary I
summary: Mary I asserted her right to the throne by inheritance and coronation, and set out to reverse the religious changes of her father and brother, restoring papal authority and Catholic worship. She revived the heresy laws, under which about 280 Protestants were burned, and married Philip of Spain despite the unpopularity of the match and a rebellion against it. Her recorded words on politics are mostly about her title, her marriage and obedience, so many topics remain without a known position.

more-religion-public.rationale: Her first measures and the Marian Restoration returned England to Catholic worship under papal obedience, and she persevered with the burnings even when advisers warned of revolt.

revolution-justified.rationale: She treated rebellion against her as treason, yet her own 1553 seizure of the throne from Jane Grey's government was framed by her as a lawful assertion of title, so the evidence is mixed.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In her Guildhall speech (Foxe's version) she claims the crown by inheritance from her father and by coronation, and her 9 July 1553 letter orders the council to proclaim her title as rightful sovereign.

political-violence-never.rationale: Mixed: in July 1553 she wished to avoid bloodshed and offered pardon, but she raised force against Wyatt and had rebels executed.

separate-church-state.rationale: She drove the reunion with Rome and the repeal of her father's and brother's church laws, so that Catholic doctrine was enforced by the crown and Parliament as the realm's religion.

restore-past-order.rationale: Her stated and enacted aim was to undo the religious changes of Henry VIII and Edward VI and restore the church as it was before the break with Rome.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Inferred: from the heresy laws she revived, which penalised adopting Protestant belief; no law on conversion as such is recorded.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Inferred: she commanded the muster against Northumberland and Wyatt and appointed her own council, though she struggled to form an effective one.

church-by-bishops.rationale: She freed and reinstated the conservative bishops, made Reginald Pole Archbishop of Canterbury in 1556 and had bishops run the heresy trials and the deprivation of married clergy.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: She did the reverse: she married Philip of Spain for a Habsburg alliance and declared war on France in 1557 alongside Spain.

death-penalty.rationale: She approved the execution of the leaders of Wyatt's rebellion, Lady Jane Grey and Suffolk for treason, after first declining to execute Jane.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: She dropped the title Supreme Head of the Church, restored papal authority, returned First Fruits and Tenths to the Church and funded the refounding of religious houses from her own money, the opposite of curbing clerical power and property.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: At the Guildhall she described herself as wedded to the realm and its laws by her coronation ring, and said she would marry only with Parliament's approval.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Contested fit: the revived heresy laws punished Protestants, including those who had returned to Protestantism, but they were framed as heresy against the Catholic church, not as a law against leaving a religion as such.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Inferred: from her claim to the throne by hereditary right, which she defended against Jane Grey and Wyatt.

elective-rulers.rationale: She based her claim on inheritance from Henry VIII, the Act of Succession and his will, not on any election by the political nation.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: She called Wyatt a vile traitor in the Guildhall speech (Foxe) and had the leaders of the 1554 rebellion executed, though the rebels objected to her marriage and policy.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Mixed evidence: she submitted her marriage and the religious repeals to Parliament, but she tried to unsettle Elizabeth's succession against Parliament's resistance.

suppress-opposition.rationale: She suppressed Wyatt's rebellion and Protestant dissent through trials and executions, but the record does not show her targeting ordinary political opposition in general (Wikipedia, Mary I of England).

punish-blasphemy.rationale: She revived the heresy laws in January 1555 and held to the burnings of about 280 Protestants despite advisers' warnings, so the open practice of what her church deemed false religion was punished by the state.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Inferred: her August 1553 proclamation, as reported by a biographer, says God had secured her crown, while her letters also rest her title on inheritance, Parliament's act and her father's will.

dynastic-succession.rationale: She hoped for a child of her own to succeed, her will named Philip regent during such a child's minority, and she told Renard it would burden her conscience to let a bastard (Elizabeth) succeed.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Her measures gave Catholic doctrine exclusive legal precedence and punished Protestant interpretations as heresy.

national-church-status.rationale: She restored the traditional Catholic church as the sole legally established church of England, though under papal rather than royal headship.

notes:
Mary's August 1553 proclamation said she would not compel subjects in religion until further order by common assent; within a year she had moved to full restoration. Statutes enacted in her name on Parliament's or ministers' advice were not counted unless she personally drove them. Foxe and chroniclers' versions of the Guildhall speech differ and are partly secondhand. Limits: the full texts of her 1554 instructions to bishops and of the proclamation were not found online in this session, so those rest on summaries.

claude-haiku-5-5 notes: Her record (restoration, heresy laws, Spanish marriage) is documented in secondary accounts; few of her own words survive, so most answers rest on what she drove. The 1553 proclamation promising not to force consciences is noted in the Wikipedia article but its wording was not retrieved, so it is not used. Chroniclers and Foxe were not opened. Counts and burnings are contested by Protestant writers; the answers follow the measures she personally drove.
